Iowa data on violent crime and arrests

Violent crime in Iowa

In 2025, 234 violent crime incidents per 100,000 residents were reported to police in Iowa. This is 15 percent lower than the violent crime rate in 2015.

The crime rate in Iowa in 2025 was 29 percent lower than the United States average.

Data regarding crime and solve rates come from the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting Program. Violent crime includes homicide, aggravated assault, robbery, and rape. Crime rates are calculated by dividing the number of estimated incidents by the total population for a given geography. For more information, see the data sources and methodology section below.

Solved violent crime in Iowa

In 2025, 59 percent of violent crimes reported to police in Iowa were solved. This is 4 percentage points higher than the solve rate in 2015.

Solve rates are the number of reported crimes cleared by arrest or by exceptional means divided by the number of reported crimes. For more information, see the data sources and methodology section below.

Law enforcement resources in Iowa

Iowa increased spending on law enforcement by 23 percent from 2014 to 2024, adjusting for inflation. Expenditures include local, state, and federal spending on local police departments, sheriffs’ offices, and state police agencies such as highway patrols and other state investigative law enforcement agencies.

Law enforcement resources also refer to the state’s staffing per 10,000 residents and per 1,000 violent crimes. These factors may show the level of policing a community receives, potentially influencing both crime and solve rates.

Additionally, the number of officers per 1k violent crimes in Iowa has increased by 27 percent from 2015 to 2025. This increase may be due to a combination of an increase in law enforcement officers and/or a decrease in reported violent crimes.

Law enforcement staffing can impact how agencies allocate resources to solve violent crime. For example, severe staff shortages can reduce investigative personnel or increase the number of cases that individual officers are managing.

NoteData sources and methodology

Data regarding crime and solve rates come from the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting Program. Statewide counts of reported violent crime between 2015 and 2025 are derived from the Summary Reporting System (SRS) and the National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS). The FBI estimates reported crime for each state from agency-level reports, accounting for agencies that did not report, and publishes these estimates on its Crime Data Explorer. Statewide solve rates apply each state’s clearance rate among agencies that reported to the FBI to the FBI’s state estimates of reported crime. The 2024 county and agency sections use Jacob Kaplan’s version of the Offenses Known and Clearances by Arrest dataset.

The FBI stopped SRS data collection after data year 2020 and required law enforcement agencies to use NIBRS to report crime statistics to the FBI. This change decreased the number of agencies that submitted their crime data and thus reduced the reliability of state estimates in 2021. The FBI later allowed agencies unable to submit NIBRS data to submit SRS data again. Comparisons involving 2021 should be interpreted with caution.

Statewide crime rates are calculated by dividing the number of estimated incidents by the total population of the state. Population data come from the U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates Program.

Solve rates are the number of reported crimes cleared by arrest or by exceptional means divided by the number of reported crimes. A reported crime incident is cleared by exceptional means if a law enforcement agency is unable to arrest or formally charge a person with a crime, but the agency has met the following conditions:

  1. Identified the person who committed the crime
  2. Gathered enough evidence to support an arrest, make a charge, and turn over the person to the court for prosecution
  3. Identified the suspect’s exact location so that the person could be taken into custody immediately
  4. Encountered a circumstance outside the control of law enforcement that prohibits the agency from arresting, charging, and prosecuting the person

Examples of exceptional clearances include the death of the person who committed the crime; the victim’s refusal to cooperate with the prosecution after the person who committed the crime has been identified; or the denial of extradition.

Annual clearances can exceed newly reported incidents because cases reported in earlier years may be cleared. As a result, annual solve rates can exceed 100 percent. The charts display rates below zero at zero and identify those values in their tooltips.

Agency- and county-level violent crime and solve rate data presented above are restricted to agencies reporting data for all 12 months in 2024. The calculation of population covered by reporting agencies, as well as the number of reporting agencies by county, is also based on agencies with violent crime data for all 12 months.

Each law enforcement agency is grouped by the county where they are based using the Law Enforcement Agency Identifiers Crosswalk developed by the Bureau of Justice Statistics in 2012. The overall county population used for calculation of county-level rates is based on the sum of the jurisdiction populations for agencies reporting data for all 12 months in 2024.

Counties with fewer than 25 reported violent incidents in 2024 are excluded from the map, as calculations of solve rates are not reliable.

Data regarding state and local police protection expenditures were downloaded from the U.S. Census Bureau Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Expenditures are adjusted to 2024 dollars using the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers.

Officer employment analysis is restricted to sworn officers in state and local law enforcement agencies and uses the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer law enforcement employee data. Officers per capita use the population served by agencies that reported employee counts. Officers per violent crime divide that rate by the state violent crime rate from the FBI state estimates.

Data on homicide solve rates and case characteristics come from the FBI’s Supplementary Homicide Reports. Solve rates combine data from 2022 through 2025. Data from 2021 are excluded because many large states did not report SHR data during the transition to NIBRS.
